newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Nigerians agree truce after Freetown strike fails.
newsitem.headline: Nigerians agree truce after Freetown strike fails.

text.p: Nigerian forces have agreed a ceasefire with coup leaders in Sierra Leone after the failure of a military strike aimed at forcing the soldiers and their rebel allies to back down.

Freetown was quiet on Tuesday after Monday's Nigerian naval bombardment sparked a punishing rebel assault on about 50 Nigerian troops cut off from their commanders guarding foreigners at a beachfront hotel.
The field commander of the regional ECOMOG force, General Victor Malu, said Nigeria would bring in jet bombers and troop reinforcements to Lungi international airport.
"We agreed a ceasefire yesterday. We hope they will respect it because if not, we are building the capacity to carry on the offensive," Malu told Reuters.

The International Committee of the Red Cross brokered a ceasefire to allow the evacuation of more than 600 civilians trapped by fighting around the Mammy Yoko Hotel. Malu said the ceasefire was now in force city-wide, and residents said there was no sign of fighting overnight.

Nigeria and Guinea, who already have ECOMOG troops in Sierra Leone, sent reinforcements after the coup, ready for a strike if talks with the coup leaders failed. They are thought to have about 3,000 men in Freetown. Ghana said it was sending troops, but only to evacuate its nationals.

Nigerian ships in the bay west of Freetown began a bombardment at dawn on Monday after talks between Nigerian and British diplomats and the coup leaders at the seafront military headquarters collapsed.

Rebels allied to the coupmakers attacked Nigerian troops at the hotel, who were hopelessly outnumbered but managed to prevent them over-running the six-storey building as the terrified civilians sheltering in the basement had feared.
The Nigerians ran low on ammunition and their communications with their commanders failed. The hotel was hit by rocket- propelled grenades and fire broke out on the top two floors.

Owners of the hotel said it was overrun by the rebels soon after the civilians were evacuated. They looted it from top to bottom and rebels drunk on the contents of the bar spent the night in the rooms.
The USS Kearsage, which steamed north from the waters off Congo to help evacuate foreigners, was expected to return on Tuesday to bring out foreigners rescued from the hotel.
Staff at Freetown's main hospital said Monday's shelling had killed 20 people in the beachside Aberdeen district.
One Nigerian at the hotel died of his wounds and 11 people were injured, mostly by shrapnel, including British defence attache Captain Lincoln Jopp.
The coup leaders had accused Kabbah of failing to consolidate a peace accord signed last November and of encouraging ethnic conflict.

Rebel leader Foday Sankoh, named as vice-chairman in Major Johnny Paul Koromah's ruling Armed Forces Revolutionary Council on Sunday, called on his men to back the coup leaders last week from his detention in Nigeria.

The Nigerian military action is increasingly controversial at home, with some newspapers supporting it but some commentators saying it lacks the moral right to attack the Sierra Leone coup makers because it is itself under military rule.
"The guys organised a successful coup and came to power like our own leaders here," said Taiwo Dopesi, a pastor. "The role we want to play does not fit us as a nation in military chains."
Nigerian authorities have not made any public statement on the issue. "This is an ECOMOG affair," said one.

Some Lagos diplomats believed that if the Nigerian-led action in Freetown succeeded in restoring the deposed president it would boost the international standing of Nigerian military leader General Sani Abacha.
Conversely: "If it ends in humiliation the consequences will be nasty not only abroad but also at home among Nigerians including the military constituency," one said.

African leaders were due to meet privately on the margins of the Organisation of African Unity summit on Tuesday to discuss what, if any, action to take on the coup, which they denounced in ringing terms at the opening session.
